content: Chemotrophs are organisms that derive their energy through the oxidation of electron-donating molecules present in their environment. These molecules can either be organic, in which case the organisms are referred to as organotrophs, or inorganic, in which case they are called lithotrophs. The term chemotroph is used in contrast to phototrophs, which rely on solar energy for their energy needs. Chemotrophs can be further classified as either autotrophic or heterotrophic. Chemotrophic autotrophs, also known as chemoautotrophs, not only obtain energy from chemical reactions but also synthesize all the organic compounds they require from carbon dioxide. These organisms typically utilize inorganic energy sources and are predominantly bacteria or archaea that thrive in extreme environments, such as deep-sea hydrothermal vents. In these ecosystems, chemoautotrophs serve as the primary producers. Evolutionary scientists hypothesize that the earliest life forms on Earth were chemoautotrophs, which produced oxygen as a by-product. Over time, these organisms are believed to have evolved into both aerobic, animal-like organisms and photosynthetic, plant-like organisms. Chemoautotrophs are generally categorized into several groups, including methanogens, halophiles, sulfur reducers, nitrifiers, anammox bacteria, and thermoacidophiles. On the other hand, chemotrophic heterotrophs, or chemoheterotrophs, must consume organic molecules because they lack the ability to synthesize these essential building blocks on their own. Most chemoheterotrophs derive their energy from organic compounds such as glucose. The terminology used to describe these nutritional groups is derived from Greek roots. The prefix chemo refers to chemical, while troph means nourishment. The term auto translates to self, and hetero means other.
